title: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) 📈
description: Automatically scale your workloads based on CPU, memory, or custom metrics.

slides.title: What is the HPA? 🤖
slides.content:
# React to load, not your pager

The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler automatically increases or decreases the number of Pods in a Deployment, StatefulSet, or ReplicaSet based on observed metrics.

By default, it uses **resource metrics** (CPU, memory) from the Metrics Server. You can also use custom metrics (e.g., requests per second) with external adapters (Prometheus, Datadog).

slides.title: Prerequisites 📋
slides.content:
## What you need

1. **Metrics Server** must be running in your cluster (many managed services have it; for minikube, enable with `minikube addons enable metrics-server`).
2. Your Pods must have **resource requests** set (HPA calculates utilisation as a percentage of the request).
3. The target resource must support scaling (Deployment, StatefulSet, ReplicaSet).

slides.title: Check Metrics Server
slides.codeSnippet:
kubectl get deployment metrics-server -n kube-system
kubectl top nodes
kubectl top pods

quizData.question: Why must Pods have CPU requests for HPA to work?

options.text: HPA uses the absolute CPU value
HPA calculates utilisation as percentage of the request

quizData.explanation: Without requests, the utilisation percentage cannot be computed.

slides.title: Creating an HPA Imperatively ⚡
slides.content:
## Quick autoscale

```bash
kubectl autoscale deployment my-deploy --cpu-percent=50 --min=1 --max=10
```

This creates an HPA that keeps the average CPU utilisation of all Pods at 50%, scaling between 1 and 10 replicas.

Check status:
```bash
kubectl get hpa
kubectl describe hpa
```

slides.title: Declarative HPA YAML 📝
slides.content:
## More control

```yaml
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: app-hpa
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: my-deploy
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 8
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: cpu
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 60
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: memory
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 80
```

You can have multiple metrics; HPA will calculate desired replicas for each and pick the highest.

quizData.question: If you define both CPU and memory metrics in an HPA, which one dictates the replica count?

options.text: The metric that yields the highest replica count

quizData.explanation: HPA takes the max desired replicas across all metrics to ensure all constraints are met.

slides.title: HPA Algorithm 🧮
slides.content:
## How it calculates

The desired replicas are calculated roughly as:
```
desiredReplicas = ceil( currentReplicas * ( currentMetricValue / desiredMetricValue ) )
```
For CPU at 50% target: if current utilisation is 80%, it would double the replicas (capped by maxReplicas).

HPA reevaluates every 15 seconds by default (configurable). It includes stabilisation windows to prevent flapping.

slides.title: Custom and External Metrics 📊
slides.content:
## Beyond CPU and memory

HPA can scale on:
- **Pods metrics** (e.g., requests per second, queue length) via the custom metrics API.
- **Object metrics** (e.g., a database connection count).
- **External metrics** (e.g., messages in a cloud pub/sub queue).

This requires an adapter like Prometheus Adapter or a cloud provider’s metrics adapter.

quizData.question: Which parameter prevents HPA from scaling up too quickly?
quizData.explanation: The stabilisation window delays scaling actions to prevent flapping.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Always set resource requests

Without requests, HPA can't compute utilization. Also, set appropriate limits to prevent a single Pod from consuming all node resources and triggering eviction.
